transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-05-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Notes link: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/steadfast (shared during call)

Summary: Quick intro, then deep into p95 targets, sample prompts, and security constraints. SE to run microbenchmarks on customer's model artifacts.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you taking the time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Mark (Steadfast CTO): Hi, Mark here — CTO. We've got Sarah from ML and Raj on platform, Anika for security.
[00:12] Maya: Awesome, Maya from Redwood. Jonas, our SE, is on to run through perf stuff.
[00:18] Jonas (Redwood SE): Hey all. We'll ask a bunch of questions, and towards the end I'll sketch an experiment plan.

[00:28] Mark: Quick context — we're building a clinician-facing assistant, mostly short prompts but sometimes long history. Our SLO is tight: p95 under 350ms for interactive flows, with bursts to 200 concurrent users during morning rounds.
[00:40] Sarah: For some flows we stream tokens (so latency matters per token), other flows we need full-document rerank which is heavier.

[00:52] Jonas: OK good, couple clarifying q's: what model family are you running now and where?
[00:58] Sarah: We're using a fine-tuned Llama-3x style model right now on our on-prem cluster — mixed across A100s and a small cluster of T4s for staging. We do some INT8 quant but not full production.

[01:18] Raj: Platform-wise we have an internal scheduler, but capacity is fragmented. Looking at Redwood to either host (fast path) or Dedicated for predictable throughput. Private deploy is interesting because of PHI rules.

[01:35] Anika (Security): We need SOC2 type II, SSO (SAML), audit logs, and KMS/HSM integration for key material. Data residency in us-east required for some datasets.

[02:00] Jonas: Sounds familiar. On p95 targets, 350ms is tight but doable depending on sequence length and quantization. We typically break the problem: cold-start latency, streaming per-token latency, and end-to-end response time.

[02:30] Maya: Can you give us typical prompt lengths and token/sec expectations?
[02:35] Sarah: Typical prompt ~120 tokens, responses around 40-120 tokens. For streaming we want <50ms per token ideally. For full rerank flows sequences hit 1k tokens occasionally.

[03:00] Jonas: OK, that clarifies. For Hosted we can often meet per-token latencies with semantic batching + prefix caching; Dedicated gives more headroom for concurrent p95. Private is constrained by your on-prem infra.

[03:30] Mark: We're most worried about the morning bursts — 200 concurrent with some long histories. Cost matters too, we don't want huge overprovisioning.

[03:45] Jonas: Two levers for cost vs latency: autoscaled Dedicated pools with reserved baseline and burst for spikes, or Hosted with routing policies to fall back to cheaper model variants. We'll quantify token/sec and cost in the spreadsheet.

[04:10] Sarah: How do you measure p95 for streaming vs full response? Sometimes streaming hides tail behaviour because first token is fast.
[04:20] Jonas: Good catch. We report both p95 first-byte and p95 end-to-end. For streaming per-token p95 we look at steady-state token latency distribution. For your use-case we should capture both.

[04:45] Maya: Can you walk through a sample benchmark plan, Jonas?
[04:50] Jonas: Sure. Step 1: run microbenchmarks on representative model and prompt set to measure tokens/sec and per-token latency across seq lengths (64, 128, 512, 1024). Step 2: run concurrency scenarios to simulate 200 concurrent sessions with mixed streaming/full responses. Step 3: validate p95 under both Hosted-equivalent (shared) and Dedicated (reserved) configs, and a Private run to emulate your on-prem disk/HPC network.

[05:20] Raj: For private runs we'd need the Redwood private agent or an on-prem package — how intrusive is that?
[05:28] Jonas: Our Private package provides a customer-managed control plane, a light-weight runtime agent; network egress minimal. It integrates with KMS for keys. There are some infra pre-reqs which I'll share.

[05:45] Anika: We need to confirm HSM compatibility and key rotation policies. Also audit log retention for 1 year.
[05:52] Maya: We'll send the Private checklist and SOC2 artifacts. Jonas, add HSM docs to that packet.

[06:10] Jonas: Will do. About quantization — you said INT8; if you can validate INT4/FP16 tradeoffs we can reduce memory footprint and increase batch sizes, but there's sometimes quality degradation. We'll test accuracy regressions tied to your eval set.

[06:40] Sarah: Quality regressions are a big concern. We need a roll-back policy if quantized model drifts.

[06:50] Jonas: Redwood Optimize offers automated regression alerts tied to your prompt set. We'll set up canary rollouts + automatic fallback to a higher-precision variant if quality drops beyond your thresholds.

[07:10] Mark: How do we handle KV/prefix cache for long histories? We can't recompute everything each time.
[07:20] Jonas: We support KV cache reuse across sessions where appropriate, and prefix caching for common conversation starters. That reduces per-token compute and lowers p95. However cache hit-rates depend on prompt variation — we'll measure this.

[07:50] Sarah: Any rough numbers — tokens/sec per GPU for our model family?
[07:55] Jonas: Ballpark: on A100 with INT8 you'd see maybe 1800-2500 tokens/sec for shorter sequences, INT4 can push more but depends on kernel support. On T4 less — maybe 400-900 tokens/sec. These are noisy numbers; microbenchmarks will pin this down.

[08:20] Mark: If we go Hosted, how do you guarantee p95? We need an SLA or at least predictable behavior.
[08:28] Maya: For Hosted we expose performance profiles and can set SLO-backed tiers. For strict p95 guarantees we recommend Dedicated pools with capacity commits or Private. We can design hybrid routes: primary Dedicated, fallback Hosted for overflow.

[08:50] Raj: Autoscaling — we need warm pools to avoid cold-start tails. How does Redwood avoid cold tails on scale up?
[08:58] Jonas: We use pre-warm policies and continuous batching so new nodes receive warmed KV cache where possible. There are also delayed-eviction policies to keep hot workers alive during predictable bursts.

[09:25] Anika: Are logs and traces available for audit? We require per-request tracing and export to our SIEM.
[09:32] Jonas: Yes, we have token-level traces, per-route dashboards, and can push to your SIEM via syslog/forwarder. We'll confirm retention windows for logs.

[10:00] Maya: Let's drill into a scenario: 200 concurrent interactive sessions with average 80-token prompts and 50-token responses, streaming enabled. What's the baseline architecture?
[10:12] Jonas: Baseline would be a Dedicated GPU pool sized to sustain steady-state QPS. We calculate tokens/sec target: assume 200 sessions * (80+50)=26k tokens per conversation over the time window — but tokens/sec depends on think-time and concurrency. For interactive with short think-time, aim for sustained 3-5k tokens/sec. We'll validate with microbenchmarks.

[10:45] Sarah: We have some variability — clinicians sometimes paste long patient history. Those tails can push latencies up.
[10:52] Jonas: That's where fallback policies matter: route long sequences to a higher-throughput model variant or to Dedicated nodes with higher batch sizes, or accept slightly higher p95 for those flows.

[11:10] Mark: What about cost modeling? We need per-hour committed vs burst pricing.
[11:18] Maya: We'll send a spreadsheet with modeled scenarios: Dedicated commit levels, burst pricing, Hosted per-token cost with discounts at volume. We'll include estimated monthly cost given your prompt mix.

[11:40] Sarah: On the microbenchmark, can you run both streaming-first-byte p95 and end-to-end p95? Also measure p99 for tails?
[11:50] Jonas: Yes, we'll capture p50/p95/p99 for first-token and end-to-end, and per-token steady-state latency.

[12:05] Raj: Network constraints on our side are another variable — our on-prem cluster has a 10Gbps interconnect; will that limit throughput?
[12:12] Jonas: It could for massive KV state transfers, but for normal inferencing 10Gbps should be fine. We'll emulate your network in Private runs to be safe.

[12:30] Maya: Any regulatory constraints besides data residency?
[12:34] Anika: PHI handling, we need encryption at rest and in transit, field-level redaction options, and proof of no persisted PII beyond logs unless explicitly stored. Also need periodic audit access.

[12:55] Jonas: We support envelope encryption and can integrate with your KMS/HSM. We'll note the redaction/retention configuration options.

[13:20] Mark: Who should we loop in for the deep dive? We'll want platform, ML, and security all present.
[13:26] Maya: Great — let's target next Tuesday; we'll reserve 2 hours. Jonas will lead the technical portion.

[13:40] Maya: Quick check — are there any competitors you're actively evaluating?
[13:44] Mark: We're talking to Anthropic, and also doing an internal proof-of-concept with our own infra. Anthropic is interesting for the hosted model.

[14:00] Jonas: Noted. We'll highlight where Redwood's Dedicated + Private options differ on latency predictability and controls.

[14:25] Sarah: For the benchmark inputs, what's the preferred format? JSONL with prompts & expected outputs?
[14:30] Jonas: JSONL with metadata, seq lengths, and a small eval set is best. Include streaming and full-response tags. Raj, if you can provide that we'll plug it into the harness.

[14:48] Raj: We'll prepare a 2000-sample set that represents morning rounds and edge-case long histories.

[15:05] Maya: Perfect. Action items recap?
[15:10] Mark: Go ahead.
[15:12] Jonas: I'll run the microbenchmarks on Redwood's infra and on a Dedicated config replica using your samples, and share the token/sec and p95 tables.
[15:20] Maya: I'll send pricing/commit options and the SOC2/Private checklist.
[15:25] Raj: I'll share the prompt JSONL and define p95 targets formally.

[15:40] Anika: We'll review the HSM/KMS specifics once you send docs.

[15:50] Maya: Any final Qs?
[15:52] Mark: No, this was helpful. Looking forward to the benchmarks.

[16:00] Jonas: One last note — we'll include quantization runs (INT8 vs FP16) and also a small eval to measure quality drift.

[16:10] Maya: Great, talk soon. Thanks everyone.

Meeting end: 16:52 UTC
